title: Bull Beats Out HPE For Next-Gen Lumi AI Supercomputer
gist: Bull (Eviden/Atos) displaced HPE as prime contractor for Finland's next-gen Lumi-AI supercomputer, a roughly $445 million AMD MI430X-based upgrade expected to deliver 10x AI performance and about 2x HPC performance versus the current Lumi-G partition at a 27.6% lower cost per teraflops than the original 2021 Lumi system, with EuroHPC's 'buy European' preference and Bull's UEC-compatible interconnect cited as key factors in the win.

themes.theme: Bull displaces HPE on Europe's flagship AI supercomputer

insights.claim: France's Bull (Eviden/Atos) beat out Hewlett Packard Enterprise to win the contract as primary contractor for the next-generation Lumi-AI supercomputer partition in Finland, ending HPE's run as main contractor for the original Lumi system.
insights.speaker: Timothy Prickett Morgan
insights.so_what: A European vendor displacing HPE on a flagship EuroHPC system signals procurement preference is shifting toward EU-based suppliers, a headwind for HPE's European HPC/AI franchise and a tailwind for Bull/Atos.
insights.locator: That CSC Finland and its EuroHPC funding arm went with Bull

insights.claim: The author attributes Bull's win largely to EuroHPC's preference to buy European wherever possible, rather than to a clear technical differentiator over HPE.
insights.speaker: Timothy Prickett Morgan
insights.so_what: If EU procurement is increasingly driven by sovereignty and industrial-policy preference rather than pure price-performance, US vendors like HPE should expect continued share loss on EU-funded HPC/AI contracts.
insights.quote: EuroHPC wants to buy European as much as possible.

insights.claim: Bull's BXI interconnect protocol is being adapted to run on Ultra Ethernet Consortium hardware, giving Bull's BullSequana XH3500 customers a choice of switching fabrics for scale-out clustering, whereas HPE's Slingshot is described as an Ethernet variant only possibly adaptable to UEC.
insights.speaker: Timothy Prickett Morgan
insights.so_what: Bull offering native UEC compatibility alongside its own BXI protocol is a genuine technical differentiator versus HPE's Slingshot as UEC standardizes AI cluster networking.
insights.locator: Bull customers using the BullSequana XH3500

insights.claim: The original Lumi supercomputer, unveiled in October 2020 with HPE as main contractor and a $237 million EuroHPC budget, delivered about 552 petaflops of aggregate FP64 compute across CPU and GPU partitions at a cost of about $431 per teraflops.
insights.speaker: Timothy Prickett Morgan
insights.so_what: The $431/teraflops baseline from 2021 is the benchmark against which Lumi-AI's cost efficiency should be judged.
insights.locator: The whole shebang was given a $237 million budget

insights.claim: The Lumi-G GPU partition, built on AMD Instinct MI250X accelerators and now over four years old, still ranked as the 11th fastest supercomputer in the world in the June 2026 Top500 rankings.
insights.speaker: Timothy Prickett Morgan
insights.so_what: A four-year-old system still holding a top-11 global ranking illustrates how much larger and more expensive newly built AI systems have become, and how durable well-designed HPC investments can be.
insights.locator: The Lumi-G partition was ranked as the number 11

insights.claim: The Lumi-C CPU-only partition achieves 82.6% computational efficiency on Linpack within a 1.22 megawatt power envelope, working out to 5.18 gigaflops per watt, versus the Lumi-G GPU partition's 53.43 gigaflops per watt on Linpack, over 10x better power efficiency than the CPU partition.
insights.speaker: Timothy Prickett Morgan
insights.so_what: The over-10x power-efficiency gap between GPU and CPU-only partitions on the same system is a concrete, sourced data point for the GPU-versus-CPU efficiency argument driving AI infrastructure capex allocation broadly.
insights.locator: which is more than 10X better power efficiency

insights.claim: The upcoming Lumi-AI partition, an upgrade to Lumi-G using AMD's MI430X (Altair) GPUs, is expected to deliver 10x the AI performance and about 2x the FP64 HPC performance of the current Lumi-G partition, per Bull and CSC Finland.
insights.speaker: Timothy Prickett Morgan
insights.so_what: A 10x AI-performance jump from a single generational GPU upgrade at similar or lower system cost sets the pace other national HPC centers will need to match to stay AI-competitive.
insights.locator: it will offer 10X the performance on AI workloads

insights.claim: About 4x of the projected 10x AI performance gain in Lumi-AI comes purely from the MI430X natively supporting FP4/FP8 precision versus the MI250X's FP16-grafted INT4/INT8, leaving roughly 2.5x from raw FP16 hardware improvement.
insights.speaker: Timothy Prickett Morgan
insights.so_what: Decomposing the performance gain shows native low-precision support, not just raw silicon improvement, is now doing much of the work in AI performance roadmaps, a reason to scrutinize whether 'generational leaps' reflect true compute gains or precision-format effects.
insights.locator: So 4X of that 10X is coming from the shift

insights.claim: The author calculates the Lumi-AI GPU partition will likely use around 991 to 1,240 nodes with roughly 4,000 to nearly 5,000 MI430X GPUs, a 58-67% reduction in node count versus the 2,978-node Lumi-G partition, while still breaking the exascale barrier at up to 1.43 exaflops peak FP64.
insights.speaker: Timothy Prickett Morgan
insights.so_what: A more than 2x reduction in physical node count for a more than 10x performance gain illustrates compute-density improvements driving down the physical and power footprint needed per unit of AI performance in next-gen systems.
insights.locator: I'm going with 1,240 nodes with 4,960 MI430X

insights.claim: Despite the roughly 60% reduction in node count, Lumi-AI is expected to consume similar or somewhat lower total system power, around 5 to 6.2 megawatts versus Lumi-G's 7.1 megawatts, because each new node draws about 2x the power of an old node.
insights.speaker: Timothy Prickett Morgan
insights.so_what: Per-node power roughly doubling even as node count drops confirms newer AI accelerators are becoming individually far more power-hungry, reinforcing the industry-wide power and cooling bottleneck theme even in efficiency-optimized upgrades.
insights.locator: Each node will, however, burn about 2X the energy

insights.claim: The Lumi-AI partition carries a price tag of €387.8 million, about $445.1 million, which against its peak 1.43 exaflops FP64 performance works out to about $312 per teraflops, a 27.6% lower cost per teraflops than the original Lumi system's $431 per teraflops in 2021.
insights.speaker: Timothy Prickett Morgan
insights.so_what: A roughly 28% cost-per-teraflops improvement over about five to six years quantifies the pace of HPC/AI cost-performance improvement that budget planners at other national labs can use as a benchmark.
insights.locator: you get a $312 per teraflops at peak

themes.theme: Multi-country funding for European AI infrastructure

insights.claim: The Lumi-AI GPU partition is expected to be installed in a new datacenter in Kajaani, Finland in the second half of 2027, funded jointly by the EuroHPC Joint Undertaking and Finland, Czechia, Denmark, Estonia, Norway, and Poland, with individual country contributions undisclosed.
insights.speaker: Timothy Prickett Morgan
insights.so_what: A six-country funding consortium behind Lumi-AI shows European AI/HPC infrastructure increasingly requires multi-nation cost-sharing to compete at scale, a model other mid-sized economies may replicate.
insights.locator: Finland, Czechia, Denmark, Estonia, Norway, and Poland

insights.claim: The broader Lumi AI factory will include a quantum computing element called Lumi-IQ, built by Finnish startup IQM Quantum Computers, which has raised €600 million in venture capital, is preparing to go public, and is currently valued at $1.8 billion.
insights.speaker: Timothy Prickett Morgan
insights.so_what: IQM's €600M raised and pending IPO at a $1.8B valuation makes it one of the better-capitalized pure-play quantum hardware startups in Europe, a name to watch for a near-term quantum IPO.
insights.locator: The quantum system is being built by IQM

insights.claim: IQM plans to install a Halocene H4 quantum system with 150 physical qubits supporting 5 logical qubits at CSC Finland in 2027, followed by error-correction upgrades in 2028, and a Halocene H5 system in 2029 delivering at least 9 logical qubits, implying roughly 270 physical qubits.
insights.speaker: Timothy Prickett Morgan
insights.so_what: A staged 2027-2029 roadmap moving from 5 to at least 9 logical qubits gives investors a concrete, dated milestone schedule to track IQM's fault-tolerance progress against competitors.
insights.locator: The plan is to installed a Halocene H4
